source.title: SLAM: Structural Linguistic Activation Marking for Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE feature mining and a subspace-dimension sweep on Gemma models, rather than the toy-network setup of the original work. Its results bear on whether structural representations can be recovered with SAEs and whether a single direction or multiple directions are effective.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the superposition literature but does not test toy-model superposition, feature sparsity or importance, or capacity-driven polysemanticity. Its watermarking results are induced by steering, so they do not establish that the same structure occurs naturally without intervention. Rows capture the paper's explicit observations about feature distribution and its k-dimension intervention results; unrelated watermark quality, robustness, and baseline comparisons are omitted.
record.test_reason: This is a watermarking paper. It takes off-the-shelf Gemma Scope SAEs as a tool, mines structural directions, steers them, and reports its own method's detection, quality and robustness. The 'distributed across 5–15 features' remark (§3.3) is an unquantified justification for using k>1. The k sweep measures watermark TPR under induced steering, not whether features are superposed, sparse or one-dimensional. No result bears on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is about watermarking. Steering structural SAE directions gives 100% TPR at about 2.3% FPR on Gemma-2 2B/9B, with a much smaller quality cost (∆Reward −1.3/−1.9) than KGW, EWD and Unigram. SLAM is robust to word-level attacks but vulnerable to syntax-restructuring paraphrase such as DIPPER. The record's point is a secondary remark: composing k=10 orthogonal SVD modes is what lets the method scale to 9B, where they say distributed representations defeat a single direction.
record.recipe_differences: The study mines SAE directions and steers them for watermarking; it does not reproduce the original toy-network feature-training method. It uses a subspace-dimension ablation as an indirect probe of representation structure.
record.method_sensitivity: Model scale and subspace dimension k change the detection outcome: k=1 reaches 100% on 2B but 90% on 9B; k=5 or 10 reaches 100% on 9B in the reported settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors assert that in Gemma-2 9B a structural concept spans 5–15 weakly-discriminative 16k SAE latents, versus a handful in 2B. Steering a single SVD mode caps watermark TPR at 90% on 9B (even at α=20) but reaches 100% on 2B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In larger models, linguistic-structure concepts are spread across more SAE latents, so single-latent steering is less effective.

record.problems: Evidence on representation geometry is indirect and tied to a watermarking intervention; only Gemma-2 2B and 9B PT models are studied for these claims. The study does not directly test superposition, sparse co-activity, feature importance, or whether the reported directions are canonical model units.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant results over the 60-row limit. The random-direction control and the many watermark quality/robustness results were not cataloged because they do not directly measure the claim versions' feature geometry.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity sweep or geometry.
All of it: no capacity or importance analysis.
The paper uses existing SAEs and does not measure feature spread across neurons or SAE recovery of features.
All of it: no completeness, stability or canonicality analysis.
No test of whether features are 1-D or multi-dimensional. The k sweep measures watermark detectability only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's own gate_note already says the paper does not test superposition, yet it labelled V4 and V6 as tested. I reclassify the study as T4: the SAE and superposition framing is background (§2.2 cites Elhage et al. as given), and every reported number is method performance. The random-direction control (TPR 16%/1%) shows that mined directions matter for steering. It is not evidence on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, more sparse features than dimensions, overlap and near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transition, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises for other reasons or is evidence of superposition.
The study tests structural feature recovery/distribution only on Gemma-2 2B and 9B; it does not measure general feature spread across neurons across LLMs or establish that these are typical models.
Completeness, stability, or canonical status of SAE features as the model's representation units.

The study compares steering with different numbers of orthogonal modes for selected structural phenomena, not whether all superposed features in LLMs are inherently one-dimensional or multidimensional.

relation.reason: Superposition motivates SAE use in §2.2; the experiments evaluate the watermarking method rather than superposition or canonical feature geometry.

tranche.reason: Uses existing Gemma Scope SAEs for watermarking and reports detection, quality, robustness and steering ablations. The structural-distribution remarks do not constitute a test of the claim versions.

source_check.notes: The listed values and cannot_determine states match the text, but these rows provide method context rather than claim-testing evidence. The approximately 2.3% FPR is an analytic Gaussian-tail calibration; Table 7's subspace rows select the best-quality α satisfying TPR ≥90%.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The study reports recoverable structural SAE features and says concepts involve co-activating or distributed features (r1–r2); it does not establish generality beyond these models or features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: One mode gives 90% TPR while k=5 and k=10 give 100%, consistent with multiple modes being useful for this induced structural signal (r7–r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: A single mode already gives 100% TPR, so the need for multiple modes is not shown uniformly across model sizes (r3–r6).
